clue.text: Unguarded hives?

blocks.note: of a person or a remark: made without a thought for the consequences, with nothing held back in reserve
the itchy raised welts of urticaria, one particular outbreak on the skin — which is what the question mark admits

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, no joinery at all, and the two senses are miles apart: one is about somebody's character, the other about their skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Unguarded is the reckless sense, acting before thinking; hives are nettle welts, so that half is definition by example of a skin eruption.

clue.text: Agreement: Everyman never to pick up musical instrument

indicators.note: In a down entry, picking a thing up carries it towards the top of the grid, so the short word beside it is written from its far end.

blocks.note: an accord is a formal agreement between parties, the word used of treaties
the setter signs these puzzles Everyman, and a setter speaking of himself is I
never is a flat refusal and so is no, which is the pair of letters that then travels upward

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'Agreement' look like a heading announcing what follows. It is the first piece of the build, and the definition is the two words at the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: musical instrument → ACCORDION: definition by example, the bellows-and-buttons squeezebox standing in for the whole category.

clue.text: Had sent off for phone component

indicators.note: Milk that has gone off has turned, and letters told they have turned will not stay in the order the clue prints them.

blocks.note: seven letters handed over whole, the past-perfect verb chosen only for what it contains

explanation.walkthrough: 'Had sent off' reads as posting a parcel, and that ordinary picture is what stops anybody counting the seven letters sitting in front of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: phone component → HANDSET: the part you lift and hold to your ear, so the definition names it as one piece of the telephone.

clue.text: Announced legal collateral package

indicators.note: To announce a thing is to say it out loud, so the clue describes a sound and leaves the spelling for you to settle.

blocks.note: the money a court holds as security for a defendant's return is bail

explanation.walkthrough: One sound, two spellings, and nothing connects them: the security a court takes and the bundle a farmer stacks share only their pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: package → BALE: a large bundle of hay, wool or cotton bound up for storage or transport, so it is one particular shape of parcel.

clue.text: Muscle collective commit crime - picked up here?

definitions.note: 'Here' only points at a place rather than naming one; the rest of the sentence says what sort of place, which is how an adverb comes to stand in for a noun.

indicators.note: A down entry runs from the top, so anything picked up is read from the bottom upward — and in the surface the same phrase means arrested.

blocks.note: the lats are the latissimus dorsi, the broad pair of back muscles gym-goers name as a group
to rob is to commit one particular crime, taking property by stealth or by force

explanation.walkthrough: A borstal was the British institution for young offenders, abolished in 1982 and still the word for where a teenage criminal was sent. Arrest in the surface, a turnaround in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: here? → BORSTAL: the question mark owns up to a bare pointer, and what the sentence points at is the place a young offender was sent after arrest.

clue.text: No-hoper, charlie abandoning one sealing deal

indicators.note: To abandon a thing is to walk away leaving it behind, and what gets left behind here is the single letter named just before the word.

blocks.note: the closer is the salesman brought in at the end to get the contract signed
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like a name in a story about a business deal, and the small c is the only sign the setter gives that it is one letter instead.
explanation.definitionFit: No-hoper → LOSER: a person with no chance of winning, the noun for somebody who fails at things rather than one who has mislaid something.

clue.text: A sneaky trick's backfiring somewhere in ancient Greece

indicators.note: A plan that backfires comes back on the person who laid it, so the pieces assembled so far are read from the far end instead.

blocks.note: the indefinite article taken as itself, one letter before anything else is done
a trap is the sneaky trick you lay for somebody, and the apostrophe-s supplies a fifth letter

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe does two jobs: in the surface it is 'is', holding the sentence together, and in the parse it is a plain S that the assembly cannot do without.
explanation.definitionFit: somewhere in ancient Greece → SPARTA: the militaristic city-state that fought Athens in the Peloponnesian War, so a vague location is answered by naming one.

clue.text: Ancient earl sporting a medal

indicators.note: To sport a hat or a badge is to wear it where it shows, so the piece named next is worn inside the other one.

blocks.note: the medal a winner takes is a gold, and the article in front of it is part of the material
E is the standard abbreviation for an earl, as printed in lists of the peerage

explanation.walkthrough: Peerage abbreviations are worth learning as a set — D for duke, M marquess, E earl, V viscount, B baron — because a title in a clue is usually just its letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient → AGE-OLD: both mean having existed for a very long time, though this one attaches to customs, questions and traditions rather than to ruins.

clue.text: Safe arrangement in which breeding comes with large bill?

blocks.note: the bird whose pouched beak is big enough to hold its own catch; the question mark allows that other birds have large bills too
breeding one strain with another is crossing them, the word a stockman or a horticulturist uses

explanation.walkthrough: A pelican crossing is the British road crossing whose lights a pedestrian presses for, named from PEdestrian LIght CONtrolled — while the surface reads as a zoo's breeding programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Safe arrangement → PELICAN CROSSING: a light-controlled place to walk across a busy road, so the definition describes it by what it is there for.

clue.text: A microlight deployed in concerning operation

indicators.note: Troops deployed are spread out into fresh positions, and letters moved into fresh positions are no longer in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: eleven letters straight from the clue; a microlight is the tiny one-person aircraft

explanation.walkthrough: Eleven letters for an eleven-letter entry is the tell, and the aviation surface — a small aircraft sent up on a mission — is doing all the work of hiding them.
explanation.definitionFit: concerning operation → LOGARITHMIC: taking a logarithm is a mathematical operation, so the adjective means belonging to that one rather than to surgery or war.

clue.text: They float topics to start conversation

blocks.note: the opening question or silly game at a party, there to get strangers talking to each other
read the first two words as ships instead: the reinforced vessels that shoulder a channel through frozen sea

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing punctuates the join, so the whole thing reads as one remark about a party; the two words at the front are a definition in their own right.
explanation.definitionFit: One half is the party sense, a topic that gets strangers talking; the other is the strengthened ship that shoulders a way through pack ice.

clue.text: Compliments looks

blocks.note: the plural noun signed at the foot of a letter — good wishes sent to somebody
the verb instead: to look at a thing steadily, or to consider it in a certain light

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and no joinery, the hardest shape a clue can take: one half is a noun, the other a verb, and nothing whatever says where the definition stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Compliments are the good wishes sent at the end of a letter; looks is the verb for viewing or considering — one word covering two parts of speech.

clue.text: Put an end to fuss about Republican games

indicators.note: About means round the outside of a thing, so the word beside it wraps itself round the two pieces that come after.

blocks.note: a to-do is a fuss or a commotion, as in 'what a to-do'
R is the letter printed beside a candidate's name on an American ballot
games at a British school is PE, the physical education lesson

explanation.walkthrough: The wrapper opens after only two letters, which is why 'fuss' looks far too short to hold anything at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Put an end to → TORPEDO: the figurative sense of sinking a plan or a negotiation outright, borrowed from what the weapon does to a ship.

clue.text: I will dance with pilots, mostly arm in arm

indicators.note: Dancing is movement that will not hold a line, so the letters gathered beside it end up somewhere other than where they started.
Mostly means all of it bar a little, and the little dropped is the final letter of the word standing next to it.

blocks.note: the pronoun taken as a single letter, the first thing thrown into the mix
six more letters lifted straight from the clue
the first of the clue's two limbs, with its last letter dropped

explanation.walkthrough: 'Arm in arm' is one warm phrase in the surface and two separate jobs in the parse: the first arm supplies two letters, the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: arm → AIR PISTOL: an arm is a weapon, so this is definition by example — one particular target-shooting sidearm standing for the general word.

clue.text: Stuck flush

blocks.note: close the gap between the two words and you have the past tense of what a bull does with its horns — pierced, and so stuck
to flush is what a face does when its owner is embarrassed, the colour rising into the cheeks

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration promises two words and the second definition needs them; the first needs the space closed up. The letters are fixed, the gaps are the setter's to move.
explanation.definitionFit: Flush is the blushing sense, colour rising to the cheeks; stuck fits the same letters read as one word, what a bull's horn does to a matador.

clue.text: Support benighted rogue

indicators.note: A rogue elephant has left the herd and does as it pleases, so the letters beside the word will not keep the arrangement they were given.

blocks.note: nine letters handed over whole; benighted means overtaken by darkness, or else ignorant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Benighted rogue' reads as a description of one shady person, and that is what stops you seeing that one of the two words is only there to shuffle the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Support → GET BEHIND: to get behind a candidate or a campaign is to back it publicly, the idiom of pushing from the rear rather than leading.

clue.text: Allow to board - and squeal

blocks.note: the conductor's sense: permitting a passenger up onto a bus or a train
to squeal is to give the game away, telling what you were meant to keep quiet about

explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes it look like a sentence interrupted, and the 'and' is the only joinery in the clue: two unrelated senses of the same two small words.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is letting a passenger climb aboard; the other is giving a secret away, which English keeps alive in the phrase 'don't let on'.

clue.text: Greek character represented by naïve type, US lawyer

blocks.note: an innocent led into something is a lamb, as in lamb to the slaughter
the DA is the district attorney, the state's prosecutor in an American court

explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' is a person in the surface and a letter of the alphabet in the parse — the commonest swap in cryptics, and worth expecting every time.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek character → LAMBDA: the eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet, so 'character' means a written symbol rather than somebody's personality.

clue.text: Maybe Hans Christian Andersen, the dog!

blocks.note: the writer of the fairy tales was born in Odense and is about as distinguished as his countrymen come; 'maybe' allows that others qualify
the second reading is the breed: the huge smooth-coated hound that stands waist-high to its owner

explanation.walkthrough: The comma invites you to read the whole thing as one exclamation about a man, and the two words after it are quietly doing a job of their own.
explanation.definitionFit: One half is definition by example, a famous Dane of the first rank; the other is the breed of very large hound that goes by the same name.

clue.text: City's wing exhausted; goal's unlikely

indicators.note: An exhausted supply has had its middle used up, so only the letters standing at either end of the word are left.
An unlikely story is one that does not hold together, and letters that do not hold together have to be put back in some other order.

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word, everything inside having gone
five more letters, with the apostrophe counting for nothing

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a match report — a winger running out of steam, a goal that will not come — and every word of it is either letters or an instruction to move them.
explanation.definitionFit: City → GLASGOW: definition by example, Scotland's largest city standing in for the general word, and the capital letter at the start of a clue signals nothing.

clue.text: Hearing sign they're talking about you?

blocks.note: the old superstition says the pair on the sides of your head give it away when you are discussed behind your back
the sign in that superstition is a sudden burning glow, which in one word is what burning makes a thing

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue leans on a folk belief rather than on any convention, and the question mark is the setter admitting as much.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearing → EARSHOT: within earshot means within the distance at which a thing can be heard, so the word names the range of somebody's hearing.

clue.text: Achieved, somewhat learnedly

indicators.note: Somewhat means to a partial degree, so what is wanted is a part of the word that follows rather than the whole of it.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters inside the long adverb, beginning one letter in from the front

explanation.walkthrough: Only two words follow the comma and the hiding place is one of them: an adverb odd enough to have been chosen for its letters rather than its sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Achieved → EARNED: the sense of having got something by deserving it — a reputation, a rest, a place — rather than merely having reached it.

clue.text: A mambo's choreographed somewhere in Kenya

indicators.note: A choreographer sets dancers moving into new positions, and the letters beside the word are moved about in exactly that way.

blocks.note: seven letters from the clue; the mambo is the Cuban ballroom dance, and the apostrophe-s gives the last of them

explanation.walkthrough: Mombasa is Kenya's old port on the Indian Ocean rather than its capital, and the clue says 'somewhere' precisely because it will not narrow the country down for you.
explanation.definitionFit: somewhere in Kenya → MOMBASA: the country's second city and its main seaport, so a deliberately vague pointer is answered by naming one place.

clue.text: Aromatic slice of flan I served

indicators.note: A slice is cut out of the middle of a thing, so a short run of letters is taken from the words that follow and the rest left alone.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters that run across both gaps, starting inside the first word

explanation.walkthrough: Three short words of a dinner-party sentence, and the run crosses two spaces — which is what makes a hidden word laid across a phrase so hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Aromatic → ANISE: an aromatic is a plant or substance with a strong scent, and this is the liquorice-flavoured seed used in baking and drinks.

clue.text: Uncapped pederero wounded woodland creatures

indicators.note: A cap sits on top of a thing, so a word uncapped has lost the letter at its front; the sporting sense, never having played for one's country, belongs to the surface.
A wounded animal moves crookedly, and letters made to move crookedly do not arrive in the order they set off in.

blocks.note: a pederero was a small ship's cannon; the P at its front is the letter the cap takes away

explanation.walkthrough: Nobody knows the word 'pederero', and that is the point: an unfamiliar string of letters sitting in a clue is nearly always there to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: woodland creatures → ROE DEER: the small native deer of British woods, a name that does not change between one animal and a herd of them.

clue.text: Stuck inside - huge blunder - avoiding reality

indicators.note: To blunder about is to stumble around with no sense of direction, so the letters named before it finish up somewhere other than where they began.

blocks.note: fifteen letters for a fifteen-letter entry, three ordinary words picked for what they contain

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunder' wants to be the noun in a sentence about a mistake, and it is the verb. The dashes chop the clue into three so the fodder never looks like one block of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: avoiding reality → DUCKING THE ISSUE: to duck is to dodge, and the idiom means side-stepping the question that actually matters instead of facing it.

clue.text: Primarily, mog's exclamation (or wail!)

indicators.note: Primarily means in the first place, so it asks for the opening letter of each word that follows, taken in the order they are printed.

blocks.note: the opening letter; a mog is British slang for a cat
the second initial, from a word that says what sort of noise is coming
even the little joining word gives up its initial
the last initial, from a word for a long complaining cry

explanation.walkthrough: Read the sentence again once the four letters are down: a cat's exclamation is exactly what you have written, which is what makes this wordplay and definition at once.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue also reads straight: a mog is a cat and this is the noise one makes, while the very same words hand over their initials.

clue.text: Season limited, did you say?

indicators.note: The question asks what was heard rather than what was written, so the entry is spelled one way and sounds like another word entirely.

blocks.note: something limited is tied — restricted, kept within bounds

explanation.walkthrough: 'Season' looks like a red herring until you remember Yuletide and Whitsuntide: the old sense survives almost nowhere else in modern English.
explanation.definitionFit: Season → TIDE: the archaic word for a season or a festival time, alive now only in Yuletide, Eastertide and the phrase 'time and tide'.
